Fresnal Shader

Normal-mapped glass sculpture inside an icy environment. This study combines environment mapping, reflection, refraction, and Schlick's Fresnel approximation to create a material that changes as the viewer interacts with it.

02 / Source material

Three inputs

The project uses the HDRI as the surrounding world and the normal map as the surface description. The rendered orb image is included as the visual target/reference for the material and composition.

Icy HDRI

An equirectangular environment image. The shader samples it as the stationary background and again in reflected and refracted directions across the object.

Surface data / iChannel0

Orb normal map

RGB values encode surface directions. These normals drive the reflection and refraction vectors. A normal-variation mask also identifies the sculpted forms.

03 / How it works

Glass Effects

The shader runs for every pixel. It does not build a mesh, instead interpreting the normal map as surface orientation and asks the HDRI what that surface would reflect or refract.

THE COMPLETE SHADER PIPELINE

How the surface turns an environment image into an icy glass material

The shader is a per-pixel rendering process. It does not construct or animate a 3D mesh. Instead, it uses the normal map as a compact description of the orb's surface, where each pixel in the map stores a direction, and that direction tells the shader how light should interact with that part of the surface.

A.

ENVIRONMENT MAPPING

First, the environment is mapped. The icy HDRI is an equirectangular image, meaning it stores a surrounding environment in a flat 2D layout. The envUV() function takes a 3D direction, normalizes it, and converts its horizontal and vertical angles into UV coordinates. Those UVs let the shader look up the color in the HDRI that lies along that direction. The same environment image is used for background,reflections, and refractions.

B.

NORMAL MAP DECODING

Next, the normal map is decoded, providing the surface orientation of the orb. Texture colors range from 0 to 1, so getNormal() remaps them into a signed vector range from -1 to 1 and normalizes the result. This gives each visible surface pixel an orientation that can be used for optical calculations.

C.

LIGHT PATH CALCULATIONS

This shader calculates two possible light paths. Reflection uses the incoming viewing ray and the surface normal to calculate the direction that the light would bounce away from the surface. Refraction calculates a transmitted direction that bends as it passes through the material. The index of refraction (IOR) controls how strongly that ray bends. Both resulting directions are converted to HDRI UV coordinates, so the shader samples the same icy environment from two different directions, one being reflected and one transmitted.

D.

FRESNEL APPROXIMATION

A glass surface does not reflect the same amount of light at every viewing angle. This shader shows how the surface reflects more light when viewed at a shallow, grazing angle, and allowing more transmitted light when viewed more directly. The shader estimates this behavior with Schlick's approximation. It calculates a base reflectance from the IOR, then adjusts that value using the angle between the view direction and the surface normal. This produces the Fresnel value used to blend the refracted and reflected HDRI samples.

E.

MOUSE CONTROLLED INTERACTIONS

In this webpage preview, moving the mouse samples different directions in the HDRI. Horizontal and vertical mouse movement shift the viewing direction used to sample the HDRI background, making the surrounding icy environment appear to move. The same input also changes the orb's viewing direction.

F.

COMPOSITING

A mask is estimated from how much each normal-map pixel differs from the map's flat background color. Pixels with little normal variation receive less of the glass treatment, while the sculpted orb, ring, and satellite bubbles receive more. The final composite blends the computed glass color over the mouse-responsive HDRI background according to this mask. This allows the shader to preserve the environment around the object while applying the reflection and refraction calculations to its surface.

In summary:The HDRI provides the world, the normal map provides the surface directions, reflection and refraction generate two environment samples, Fresnel balances them, and the mask places the result into the final image.

04 / Reference study

Class Examples

The implementation adapts the concepts shown in Professor Akleman's provided shader references into one focused icy-glass scene.

REFERENCE CONCEPT

Normal map + environment map

The examples reiterate the workflow of decoding a normal map, using the resulting surface direction to calculate optical vectors, and looking up the environment map to obtain reflected or refracted color.

REFERENCE CONCEPT

Fresnel-based optical blending

The project uses the angle-dependent reflectance idea and Schlick approximation to combine reflected and transmitted environment samples instead of treating the surface as uniformly reflective.

MY ADAPTATION

Mouse-Responsive Environment

Mmouse input shifts the direction used to sample the HDRI. This creates an interactive environment in which the icy landscape moves alongside changes to the orb's viewing and optical directions.

MY ADAPTATION

One composition from a normal-map

This shader uses the supplied normal-map image as a 2D surface description. A normal-variation threshold creates a soft mask for the main orb, ring, and smaller bubbles.
